chunks: From him, from Abu Ja'far, from Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both), who said:

I asked him about a man and a woman who dye (their hands) with henna and khubaz (indigo), do they pray while they are with the henna and khubaz? He said, 'If they expose the mouth and the nostrils, there is no harm (in their prayer).'

key_terms.فَلَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm (it is permissible/valid)
key_terms.يَخْتِضَانِ: They dye (specifically with henna or indigo)

ai.seo_question: Does henna or indigo on the hands invalidate prayer in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the distinction between mere coloration and a physical barrier in the context of wudu, affirming that natural dyes like henna and khubaz do not invalidate prayer as long as they do not prevent water from reaching the mouth and nostrils. It reflects the Shia juristic principle that thin layers of dye are permeable, contrasting with substances like thick paint or glue that form an impermeable barrier. This ruling is foundational for understanding the conditions of 'ghasr' (blocking) in ritual purity.
